To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the uptake of hypericin into the tumor mass is a function of tumor size, blood flow, and vessel permeability.
the accumulation of hypericins in tumours is determined by a combination between tumour blood supply, vessel permeability, and affinity for the interstitial space.

(i) hypericin accumulates rapidly and in high amounts in tumours, (ii) the tumour accumulation is critically dependent on tumour weight and on blood flow and vessel permeability, (iii) lipoproteins play a key role in the transport of the drug in tumours.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the tumouritropic behaviour of the photosensitizer hypericin.
the elucidation of the tumouritropic principle of the photosensitizer hypericin.
the elucidation of the mechanism of hypericin uptake by tumours, and with the identification of the factors that determine the accumulation and dispersion patterns of the drug.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hypericin, in its lipoprotein complex, is rapidly transported through the tumour vasculature, and is then released from the lipids and diffused through the interstitial fluid.

hypericin, like other photosensitizers, has a dual behaviour, with a first rapid phase in which it is transported in the bloodstream and a second slow phase in which it migrates through the interstitial fluid.
hypericin, in its tumouritropic behaviour, behaves as a classical lipophilic drug.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hypericin is a promising photosensitiser in photodynamic therapy of solid tumours, but the use of lipoprotein-bound hypericin in tumour treatment is not advisable.

the tumouritropic principle of this photosensitizer is based on its lipoprotein-mediated transport, which allows it to reach a large number of tumour cells, while its subsequent dispersion in the interstitial space ensures a homogeneous distribution of hypericin throughout the tumour.
hypericin, a highly lipophilic molecule, has an affinity for lipoproteins, which are present at high concentration in the tumour interstitium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the accumulation of hypericins and other photosensitisers in tumours is determined by a number of biological factors and not just the tumour vasculature.

the use of hypericin alone or in combination with lipoproteins as a photodynamic agent should be considered with caution, as the tumour uptake and dispersion of hypercin is highly variable from one tumour model to the other.

the tumouritropic behaviour of hypericin, and possibly other tumour-targeted photosensitisers, is determined by a complex interplay between biological and physicochemical factors, which may have important implications for the design of new generation photosensitisers.
